name: LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)
baseline: STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index")
workload: Point lookups/inserts on four datasets (Longitudes 1B, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M keys) under Read-Only, Read-Heavy, Write-Heavy, Write-Only workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x throughput vs ALEX/PGM/Learned-Index/B+Tree on read-only workloads; 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x vs ALEX/PGM/B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i7 (4 cores, 8 threads) @ 4.0GHz, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, single thread used
tradeoffs: No concurrency support; amortized O(log^2 N) insert cost vs B+Tree's better worst case; needs periodic subtree adjustment; benefit shrinks a lot on highly non-uniform key distributions
caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only; gains vary strongly by dataset (as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset); repo unmaintained since Feb 2022
found_via: GitHub code search 'updatable learned index' + citation from the PGM-index/ALEX literature; verified via PVLDB paper PDF (Sections 6.1-6.2)

name: ALEX (Adaptive Learned indEX)
baseline: STX B+Tree (std::map-like ordered index); also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a 2-stage RMI ("Learned Index"), and a Model-enhanced B+Tree
workload: Point lookups/inserts on 4 real datasets (longitudes, longlat, lognormal, YCSB; 200M 8-byte keys) under read-only and read-write (mixed insert) workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x higher throughput and 800x/15x/160x/8000x smaller index than B+Tree/Learned-Index/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-only workloads; up to 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x higher throughput and 2000x/475x/36000x smaller index vs B+Tree/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K 3.6GHz, 64GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
stars_or_usage: 701 stars; used as a baseline by many follow-up learned-index papers (LIPP, CARMI, etc.)
tradeoffs: No concurrency support in the public implementation; can degrade under adversarial/skewed insert patterns without retraining; README explicitly calls it 'a near drop-in replacement for std::map'
caveats: Hardware stated in the SIGMOD'20 paper (arXiv preprint) but compiler/optimization flags not given in the accessible text; independently reused as a baseline by later peer-reviewed papers (LIPP, CARMI), which corroborate the B+Tree comparison
found_via: Starting query variation: 'in-memory learned index drop-in replacement std::map faster than B-tree'

name: PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)
baseline: 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index); also matches a cache-efficient B+-tree and CSS-tree at far less space
workload: Point queries on a Web Logs dataset (~715M timestamps, 8-byte keys, 128-byte payload), 10M random queries against an in-memory sorted array index
claimed_speedup: PGM-index matches the fastest B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB) and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 83x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); at matched space, PGM-index dominates a 2-stage RMI in latency
hardware: 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold CPU, 192 GiB memory
stars_or_usage: 874 stars; basis for the PyGM Python wrapper, widely cited in follow-on learned-index papers
tradeoffs: Base structure targets static/append-friendly data (a dynamic variant exists but adds complexity); requires a sorted key array; the headline win vs traditional trees is space at matched latency, not a raw query-latency multiplier
caveats: VLDB'20 paper states hardware but not compiler/flags; the clear throughput/latency win over a named baseline is specifically vs RMI, while the B+-tree/CSS-tree comparisons are same-speed-less-space rather than strictly faster
found_via: GitHub topic search 'learned index' + citation chain from the LIPP and CARMI papers

name: CARMI (Cache-Aware RMI)
baseline: STX B+Tree and ALEX; also beats RMI on the SOSD benchmark platform
workload: Point lookups/inserts on 7 datasets (uniform, lognormal, YCSB, OSM, Facebook, ~10^8 keys) under read-only/write-heavy/read-heavy/write-partial/range-scan workloads, single-threaded, 100k operations per workload
claimed_speedup: Average 2.2x/1.9x speedup vs B+Tree/ALEX while using only ~0.77x the memory of B+Tree; on the SOSD platform CARMI beats all baselines with an average 1.2x speedup over the nearest competitor, RMI
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X 8-core CPU, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
tradeoffs: Read/static-friendly cost model; construction is more expensive due to a cost-based dynamic-programming search; gains shrink on already cache-friendly small datasets
caveats: Very low adoption (10 stars) and repo has not been updated since Jan 2022; numbers come from the authors' own paper, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB)
found_via: gh search repos 'cache aware learned index' -> embryo-labs/CARMI, cross-checked against the arXiv preprint (2103.00858)

name: SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)
baseline: RocksDB (its built-in Bloom filter used as the SSTable filter)
workload: RocksDB Open-Seek and Closed-Seek range queries over a synthetic 2K-sensor time-series dataset (~100GB raw records), comparing SuRF-Real/SuRF-Hash filters vs RocksDB's default Bloom filter
claimed_speedup: SuRF-Real speeds up Open-Seek queries by 50% and Closed-Seek queries by up to 5x (at 99% empty-result queries) vs RocksDB's Bloom filter, by cutting I/Os per operation
hardware: Intel Core i7-6770HQ CPU, 32GB RAM, Intel 540s 480GB SSD
stars_or_usage: 554 stars; SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper; RocksDB integration fork published at efficient/rocksdb
tradeoffs: It is a range filter, not a full ordered index; false-positive rate depends on how many suffix bits are used; adds per-SSTable construction overhead; only helps when the underlying block read would otherwise be wasted
caveats: Benefit is I/O reduction rather than raw CPU throughput; speedup is workload/skew dependent; repo unmaintained since 2022
found_via: gh search code 'range filter' + repo README link to the RocksDB integration experiments

name: Adaptive Radix Tree (rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree)
baseline: std::map (red-black tree, libstdc++) -- the closest stdlib ordered-index analog to the assignment's B-tree baseline
workload: 1.6M sparse 64-bit keys; delete/insert/mixed/query (uniform and Zipfian) micro-benchmarks comparing art::art vs std::map vs std::unordered_map
claimed_speedup: ~1.5x-2.1x faster than std::map on delete (1.985x), insert (2.118x), mixed (1.824x), query-uniform (1.517x) and query-zipf (1.817x); slower than std::unordered_map on delete/query, roughly at parity on insert/mixed
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 (copyleft) limits use in permissively-licensed or proprietary code; slower than std::unordered_map for pure lookups/deletes in this benchmark; only sparse-key workload shown
caveats: No compiler flags or CPU model stated for the benchmark numbers; it is the project's own micro-benchmark (uses nanobench-style harness), not an independent suite
found_via: gh search repos 'adaptive radix tree' sorted by stars

name: libmdbx
workload: CRUD benchmark suite (ioArena, 'make bench-quartet') run against an in-tmpfs database, comparing libmdbx vs LMDB (and optionally RocksDB/WiredTiger)
claimed_speedup: 10-20% faster than LMDB in tmpfs CRUD benchmarks; up to 30% faster than LMDB when compiled with build options that downgrade certain runtime checks to match LMDB's behavior
stars_or_usage: 1.4k+ stars; README claims use in hundreds of open source projects including Ethereum clients
tradeoffs: Slower than LMDB on Windows due to native file locking; larger feature surface than LMDB increases complexity; the canonical project has moved off GitHub and this is now a mirror/transfer
caveats: Benchmark is reproducible via the separate ioArena tool, but no CPU model or compiler flags are given alongside the claim; original canonical repo was erthink/libmdbx, which GitHub now redirects to Mithril-mine/libmdbx
found_via: GitHub topic search 'lmdb alternative faster' -> erthink/libmdbx (now Mithril-mine/libmdbx)

name: redb
baseline: RocksDB and SQLite (also benchmarked against LMDB and fjall, with mixed results)
workload: Embedded KV benchmark: bulk load, individual/batch writes, len(), random reads/range reads at 1/4/8/16/32 threads, removals, on-disk size; redb vs lmdb, rocksdb, fjall, sqlite
claimed_speedup: Individual writes: 920ms vs RocksDB 2432ms and SQLite 7040ms (~2.6x/7.7x faster); random reads: 1138ms vs RocksDB 2911ms and SQLite 4283ms (~2.6x/3.8x faster, derived from page data); redb loses to LMDB on most read-heavy rows in the same table
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9950X3D CPU, Samsung 9100 PRO NVMe SSD
tradeoffs: Rust, only usable from C++ via FFI; consistently slower than LMDB on random/range reads and on removals; larger on-disk size than RocksDB/SQLite in this benchmark
caveats: The project's own README says redb has only 'similar' performance to LMDB overall -- LMDB wins most read-heavy rows in the very table being cited; the clear win is specifically vs RocksDB and SQLite, not LMDB. Hardware is stated, compiler/build flags are not.
found_via: gh search repos 'embedded key value store rust lmdb rocksdb' sorted by stars

name: TerarkDB
baseline: RocksDB v6.12 (TerarkDB is a fork/drop-in replacement of RocksDB v5.18.3)
workload: db_bench with 10 client threads, 20GB requests/thread, 24-byte keys / 2000-byte values, heavy_write (90% writes) and heavy_read (90% reads) workloads on NVMe SSD
claimed_speedup: TerarkDB outperforms RocksDB v6.12 on the heavy_write and heavy_read db_bench workloads per the README's 'Performance Overview' bar chart; only shown graphically, not as an exact quoted multiplier
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 5218 CPU @ 2.30GHz (32 cores/64 threads), 376GB DRAM, NVMe TLC SSD (3.5TB)
tradeoffs: Linux-only / production-ready claim is Linux-specific; non-C/C++ language bindings not fully tested; migration back to plain RocksDB from TerarkDB is not supported; optional TerarkZipTable adds a libaio dependency
caveats: Numbers are presented only as a bar-chart image (compare_rocksdb.png) in the README rather than exact text figures; no compiler/flags stated
found_via: gh search repos 'rocksdb compatible faster' sorted by stars

name: ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against
workload: Concurrent lookup/insert/remove throughput at up to 20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention), plus lookup/insert at 20 threads on three string datasets (genome 256K keys, Wikipedia 16M titles, URL 6.4M URLs), comparing ART synchronization variants (Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) vs Masstree
claimed_speedup: ROWEX/Optimistic Lock Coupling beat Masstree by roughly 2x on lookup/insert throughput for the genome and URL string datasets at 20 threads; Masstree is faster on the Wikipedia dataset and closes the gap with longer keys
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W v3 (Haswell EP, 10 cores/20 threads), 25MB L3 cache
tradeoffs: Requires jemalloc and TBB; ROWEX needs custom epoch-based memory reclamation and is the most complex variant to implement/maintain; the paper itself notes the ART-vs-Masstree comparison is not apples-to-apples since the synchronization protocols and data structures differ
caveats: Results are mixed across datasets (Masstree wins on the Wikipedia string dataset); Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines; the last GitHub push (2026-05-24) is likely a housekeeping commit on an otherwise ~2015-era codebase, so treat 'active' loosely
found_via: GitHub topic search 'adaptive radix tree concurrent' -> cross-referenced against the ART synchronization DaMoN 2016 paper
